articles.title: Core inflation measures can't escape high energy prices
articles.text:
Core inflation measures can't escape high energy prices
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 20, 2026
Core inflation measures can't escape high energy prices
Somewhere between 0.2% and 0.6% of inflation in core PCE over the past year is the product of high energy costs, according to a Dallas Fed report.
Economyby Elizabeth Trovall
Download
Because almost every consumer good requires transportation (and thus fuel), it has become harder to separate elevated energy costs from other inflation.
Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images
Core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) is an inflation measure that is supposed to strip out the cost of food and energy because they’re so volatile — something the U.S. has been experiencing for a while now.
But a new report from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas shows that higher energy prices are showing up even in core PCE. It’s 3.1% higher than a year ago. Fed economists estimate that between 0.2% and 0.6% of that are the knock-on effects of high fuel prices.
“Ultimately, energy costs have to work their way through the entire ecosystem,” said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategy director at U.S. Bank. “There's not much that shows up at our house or at our store without requiring a fossil fuel to get there.”
Often, energy costs permeate the ecosystem through producer prices — the costs businesses charge each other.
“If the transportation company or the the maker of the product — or ultimately the the retail store at the end — if they think they can raise prices and still sell as many units of of whatever, they will pass that cost along,” Haworth said.
Diesel — which has been especially expensive — is a major contributor, according to Ed Hirs, an economics lecturer the University of Houston.
“Typically, no one can can eat the increased cost of fuel — especially diesel — because it permeates the economy,” Hirs said. “It is passed through all the time.”
The price of transportation services has been particularly sensitive to fuel costs.
“When you think about transportation, you have to think about public transportation,” said Olu Sonola, U.S. head of economic research at Fitch Ratings. “You have to think about airfares. You have to think about buses and rail. Ultimately, they need energy.”
Sonola said that companies across the board generally seem comfortable passing along their higher prices.
“Consumers continue to spend, and until we get to a point where consumers truly push back — which also which basically means demand starts to weaken — you're not probably not going to get rid of the inflationary pressures we're seeing,” Sonala said.

The big news of the week was AI, with Anthropic’s historic public debut on Thursday. Following that mega-IPO, tech stocks took a turn for the worse, and selloffs continued into Friday.
The rest of the economy kept itself busy while the stock market tumbled. President Donald Trump took a trip to China. Retail sales came in hot, rising 7% in October year-over-year. Federal Reserve governors across the country gave speeches, signaling a rate hike to come.
To cover all that and the rest of the week’s economic news, “Marketplace” host Kai Ryssdal spoke with Sudeep Reddy, Washington bureau chief at MS NOW, and Catherine Rampell, economics editor at The Bulwark, for the Weekly Wrap.

What the Deutsche Bank leak revealed

Donate

What you need to know about the Deutsche Bank leak
New documents illuminated more about the German bank’s business with sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Companiesby Kimberly Adams, Tamar Faggen and Ariana Rosas
Download
Above, the headquarters of Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt, Germany.
Thomas Lohnes/Getty Images
A new flood of leaked documents is putting fresh scrutiny on Deutsche Bank, which just reported a third consecutive quarter of record profits.
The documents include more than 15 million internal emails and files, covering the early 2010s through 2021. A group of more than 200 journalists across media outlets across the globe has been analyzing the leaked information, revealing questionable practices, deals with Russian oligarchs, and more.
The investigation is called Inside Deutsche Bank, and Dan McCrum, a reporter at the Financial Times, is among the journalists involved. He recently spoke with “Marketplace Morning Report” host Kimberly Adams about the reporting. The following is an edited transcript of their conversation.
Kimberly Adams: Can you briefly describe the role that Deutsche Bank plays in the global banking industry?
Dan McCrum: This is one of the most systemically important banks in the world. It's a huge investment bank. It's an enormous retail bank for everyday people in Germany, but also it's one of those key nodes in the financial system for moving money around. So it deals with more than $1 trillion worth of international money transfers every single day.
Adams: Even though this is a German bank, your investigation revealed new information about some high-profile Americans. What did you find?
Deutsche Bank "deals with more than $1 trillion worth of international money transfers every single day," said Financial Times investigative reporter Dan McCrum.
Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
McCrum: Well, one of the sort of funny things about this story is there's a string of disasters inside the bank to do with technology, and one of them is that during President Trump's first administration, the bank accidentally sends a load of his tax information out to an accountant, along with a whole load of other clients, including some of them connected to the president.
Adams: And there were also new revelations in your investigation about Jeffrey Epstein and his connections to the bank.
McCrum: So the notorious pedophile was one of Deutsche Bank's, I guess, most infamous clients, and it kind of signifies how this bank, for a long time, chased business with people who other banks wouldn't touch. And what we've discovered in this leak of documents is that its business with Jeffrey Epstein was even bigger than we realized — sort of, the number for the amount of transactions it was involved in is almost $600 million worth. That's double what we previously knew.
Adams: How has the bank responded to your investigation so far?
McCrum: I mean, the bank says it has changed fundamentally since its chief executive, Christian Sewing, took over in 2018; he has dealt with all these problems, and that this is old news, we're digging through stories that people knew. In some sense, you know, Deutsche Bank is famous for the huge number of scandals that it ran into in the 2010s, and it's trying to play this down as things which happened in the past. And I would say, well, you know, there are quite a few interesting things which have carried over into the 2020s, and you know, there are decisions under Christian Sewing that I think are worth looking at a little bit more closely, that perhaps he has continued the Deutsche tradition of, at times, sweeping problems under the rug.
Adams: So, what should we be watching for as the rest of the reporting comes out?
McCrum: I think there are still some very interesting stories to come that are going to, I think, surprise people. I mean, some of the details. I think it's the accretion of things that can really matter.

What Black unemployment says about the labor market
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 19, 2026
The labor market might be OK, but there are signs of stress
The Black unemployment rate was sliding throughout this past summer, but then it jumped up a full percentage point in September.
Equityby Kai Ryssdal and Sean McHenry
Download
Joe Raedle/Getty Images
The labor market looks pretty OK right now. According to the October jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the economy added 165,000 jobs. The unemployment rate slid down a little to 4.1%. Lots of sectors are hiring.
But that doesn’t mean there aren’t things to watch, said Gbenga Ajilore, chief economist at the Center on Policy and Budget Priorities — especially when it comes to Black women.
“If you look at the other kind of metrics of like labor force participation, those are pretty good,” said Ajilore. “But then if you split it by gender, you see that Black women are starting to struggle, especially with being able to find a job, and that the share of Black women with a job has been going down over the last couple months.”
“Marketplace” host Kai Ryssdal spoke to Ajilore about the data on Black workers and Black women, and what he’ll be watching in the coming months.
To listen, use the media player above.

articles.title: Unpaid caregiving is taking an economic toll
articles.text:
SNL 'Sister' skit gets at the toll of unpaid caregiving
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 19, 2026
Unpaid caregiving is taking an economic toll
KFF reports that three in 10 adults have cared for an elderly, disabled, or chronically ill friend or family member in the last year.
Equityby Mitchell Hartman
Download
seb_ra/Getty Images
There’s a “Saturday Night Live” sketch making the rounds on social media: a fake ad with a middle-aged guy musing about what to do with his befuddled old dad, who can’t take care of himself anymore.
“You know, that SNL skit went viral; I’ve had 30 different people send it to me,” said Liz Hamel, director of public opinion research at KFF, the nonprofit health research organization. “ This resonates so broadly.”
KFF has a new survey out on unpaid caregiving, which finds that three in 10 adults have taken care of an aging, disabled, or chronically ill friend or family member in the last 12 months. About a quarter of those folks spend 15 hours a week doing it; nearly half work full-time.
And the gender gap that the SNL skit portrays is real. KFF’s report finds the majority of unpaid caregivers are women.
“Women ages 50 to 64 — four in 10 of them told us that they’ve been a caregiver in the past year,” Hamel said. “Especially women who are working full-time, they were much more likely than their male counterparts to say that their own mental and physical health had suffered.”
Overall, for both men and women, “about a quarter say that they’ve experienced financial strain or employment impacts,” Hamel said.
Duke University health economist Courtney Van Houtven said that, with an aging population, unpaid caregiving is desperately needed. But it’s not really free.
“We are paying a high cost. There are a lot of labor market effects,” Van Houtven said. “People have to reduce work, which reduces tax revenues. Youth caregivers give up their schooling and don’t go to college. Women retire too early, or they get passed over for promotions.”
And that means they end up saving less for retirement and to pay for long-term elder care when they’ll need it most.

articles.title: Why this family is leaving Idaho for good
articles.text:
Anti-trans laws are driving this Idaho family out of the state
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 5, 2026
Why this family is leaving Idaho for good
“You live the life you have, not the one you dreamed of,” said Michael Devitt, who recently closed down his Idaho-based business.
My Economyby Maria Hollenhorst
Download
Michael Devitt with his family. Devitt recently closed down his physical therapy office as part of the process of leaving the state of Idaho.
Courtesy Devitt
Michael Devitt had a vision for his retirement. After three decades of practicing physical therapy in downtown Boise, Idaho, he and his three employees would close their office together and retire.
“We were going to run through the tape in probably four years,” Devitt said. “But you know, you got to live the life you have, not the life you dreamed of. I guess.”
Things changed for Devitt earlier this year, after Idaho’s Gov. Brad Little signed into law a bill criminalizing transgender people for using bathrooms that align with their gender identity.
Devitt’s daughter is transgender.
“That completely changed not the way we saw Idaho, but the way Idaho saw our family,” he said.
A federal judge blocked that specific law, but it came after a series of legislative actions aimed at restricting transgender Idahoans.
“That made us have to rethink our relationship with the state of Idaho, and me in particular, my work situation and my private practice clinic that I had owned for 28 years.”
To hear the rest of Devitt’s story, click the audio player above.

articles.title: Cars aren't getting any more affordable
articles.text:
Why car prices just keep climbing
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 19, 2026
Cars aren't getting any more affordable
A new report from Edmunds says the average price for a new car has finally crested $50,000.
Retailby Caleigh Wells
Download
New car buyers are taking out longer-term loans to afford the rising costs.
Scott Olson/Getty Images
The average price of a new car just surpassed $50,000, according to a report from Edmunds. That’s after you take the typical discount of a couple thousand dollars off the sticker price.
Despite that eye-watering average, people are still buying them — they just afford them by spreading out the payments. More than a quarter of new-car buyers are signing up for seven-year car loans, or longer.
Art Wheaton was excited to buy the new, cheap, Ford pickup truck. But then Ford released it and the price tag was higher than he thought it’d be. And that keeps happening.
“If you get rid of all the cheaper cars, all of a sudden the average price goes up as well,” he said.
Wheaton is a professor at Cornell University, and studies the auto industry. He said since wealthy people keep buying new cars, carmakers focus on making luxury cars.
On top of that, nobody buys the base model anymore, said Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds.
“You've already decided the model you like the way it looks, but now it comes down to packages. Do you want an appearance package? You want a winter package? You want a sun and sound package?” he said.
He said once a driver has had a car with remote start and climate-controlled seats, they don’t want to give that up. So they pay more.
“People are packing on something close to like 30% in options alone,” Drury said.
As for what’s next? Ray Shefska, co-founder of CarEdge, is baffled that car prices just keep going up.
“We keep saying, ‘it's not sustainable.’ It's not sustainable, but it is, and it has been, and it continues to be,” he said.
Shefska said at this point, he doesn’t think the average price will stop going up any time soon, because of the people who can pay sticker price.
“Ultimately, the chasm between the haves and the have-nots in this country has never been wider,” he said.
But just because consumers are shelling out doesn’t mean they aren’t looking for ways to save. Edmunds also says hybrid cars’ market share is up 25%, year over year.
